description: DeltaSky is a solo team, building a public web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Built with Python, JAVA, Html, FastAPI, Astropy, and Aladin Lite, it uses NASA IRSA SPHEREx data for multi-epoch image subtraction and 102-band near-IR spectrum plotting to help anyone spot moving objects. Solo entry—team is complete and not seeking additional members
summary:
I developed SPHEREx Chronoscope, a public-facing web application that transforms NASA SPHEREx's 102-band near-infrared all-sky survey (0.75–5.00 µm) into an interactive time-domain discovery engine for spotting fast-moving brown dwarfs, comets, variable stars, and Planet X candidates.

Users can query any sky patch by object name, decimal, or sexagesimal RA/Dec coordinates (or shareable URL query parameters), choose custom fields of view (1.5'–12'), and inspect multi-epoch observations as an animated blink video. To surface faint or shifting sources, DeltaSky uses Astropy to reproject Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) data onto a unified WCS grid, perform inverse-variance co-addition across SPHEREx's six detector arrays, and run interactive epoch subtraction (e.g., QR3 − DR1) that exposes proper-motion dipoles and variable-star monopoles. Clicking any pixel generates an on-the-fly 102-band spectrum with H2O, CH4, CO2, and CO molecular band overlays, paired with Gaia DR3 and AllWISE proper-motion vectors, contamination bitmask flags, FITS export, and live NASA IRSA SIAv2 querying with resilient offline fallbacks.

Validated on Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis, DeltaSky lowers the barrier for citizen scientists worldwide to make new discoveries across more than a billion SPHEREx objects.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

SPHEREx Chronoscope is an interactive, web-based time-domain exploration tool built for NASA's SPHEREx near-infrared all-sky survey (102 spectral bands across 6 detector arrays from 0.75 to 5.00 µm).

• Coordinate & Target Resolution: Users enter any sky patch in decimal degrees, sexagesimal coordinates (e.g., 08h55m10.831s -7d14m42.53s), object name, or via shareable URL parameters (?ra=...&dec=...&fov=...). One-click presets test all five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

• Multi-Epoch Alignment & Blink Video: Backend Astropy WCS routines reproject rotated and dithered Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) epochs (QR1, DR1, QR2, QR3) onto a unified North-up tangent grid and stream an interactive blink movie (Play/Pause, frame scrubber, 0.5–8.0 FPS).

• 6-Array Co-Addition & Epoch Subtraction: Users can co-add all 102 bands or isolate any individual detector array (Arrays 1–6) via inverse-variance weighting to boost signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). An interactive subtraction mode (Epoch B − α·Epoch A, such as QR3 − DR1) cancels stationary stars to reveal moving brown dwarfs as red/blue dipoles and variable stars as bright monopoles.

• On-the-Fly 102-Band Spectroscopy: Clicking any pixel extracts its full 0.75–5.00 µm spectrum with variance error bars, multi-epoch comparison (DR1 vs QR3), and H2O, CH4, CO2, and CO molecular band overlays.

• Multi-Mission Overlays & Diagnostics: Overlays Gaia DR3 (with 2016-to-2026 proper-motion vectors) and AllWISE catalogs, decodes FITS contamination bitmasks (BAD_PIXEL, COSMIC_RAY, PERSISTENCE, ZODI_HIGH, STRAY_LIGHT), and lets researchers export WCS-aligned FITS cutouts.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

SPHEREx maps more than a billion objects every six months, far exceeding what astronomers can visually inspect alone. By turning raw multi-extension spectral data into an intuitive blink comparator, difference-imaging workspace, and instant spectrometer—embeddable in citizen-science portals via URL query parameters or (iframe)—Chronoscope empowers volunteers and researchers worldwide to discover new brown dwarfs, comets, variable stars, and outer Solar System bodies (including Planet X candidates).

3. Tools, Languages & Software Used

• Backend & Astrophysics Pipeline: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy (WCS, SkyCoord, io.fits, io.votable), NumPy, SciPy (ndimage.map_coordinates), Astroquery (VizieR Gaia DR3 & AllWISE), PyVO / HTTPX (NASA IRSA SIAv2), PyYAML, and Pydantic.

• Frontend & Visualization: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, Plotly.js (interactive heatmaps, blink animation, and 102-band spectra), and CDS Aladin Lite v3.

• Data Protocol: NASA/IPAC IRSA Simple Image Access v2 (SIAv2) targeting COLLECTION="spherex_dr1" and multi-epoch releases, paired with local Multi-Extension FITS benchmark/fallback cubes.

• Development Environment & AI Assistance: Visual Studio Code (VS Code), Python virtual environments (.venv), and Google AI Studio (used as an architectural, prototyping, code scaffolding and debugging assistant during development).

• Hosting & Version Control: GitHub, Render

4. Creativity & Design Factors Considered

• Detector-Physics Awareness: Extreme cold Y-dwarfs like WISE 0855 (~250 K) vanish in optical/short-NIR bands (Array 1) but glow brightly in thermal bands (Arrays 5–6). Isolating arrays makes these temperature contrasts immediately visible.

• Rapid Data-Release Extensibility: An externalized config.yaml and an in-app "+ Add Data Release" modal allow researchers to register newly published IRSA collections (such as future DR2/QR4 releases) with zero code changes.

• FOV vs. Transfer Tradeoff: Users choose fields of view from 1.5' to 12.0' with live pixel-grid and transfer-size estimates to balance fast-mover tracking against bandwidth.

• Network Resilience: Strict timeouts and automatic fallbacks prevent crashes if IRSA SIAv2 is slow/unpopulated or if external CDS Aladin servers are unreachable on restricted networks—switching seamlessly to a built-in J2000 Sky-Context chart and cached MEF FITS cubes while logging full query provenance.
